body.text: Every so often, a high-profile case of domestic violence sparks a wave of discussion – largely in social and traditional media – across Central Asia. Violence and against women, and other forms of sexual and gender-based violence are sensitive topics, but in recent years many regional governments have taken steps toward addressing these issues.
In Tajikistan, for example, the Law on the Prevention of Domestic Violence was passed in 2013. But enforcement is weak and cultural stigma surrounding domestic violence remains.

In a recently published study, Nushofarin Noziri, a gender and security expert, examines media coverage of violence against women in Tajikistan in an effort to understand how public perceptions are formed.

In the following interview with The Diplomat’s Managing Editor Catherine Putz, Noziri explains her research and explores how media and law enforcement in Tajikistan can do better in covering and responding to cases of sexual and gender-based violence.
What role does media, especially digital and social media, play in shaping public perceptions and policy responses to violence against women in Tajikistan?

Tajikistan’s population is increasingly online. People use Facebook, Instagram, Telegram, and other platforms to discuss pressing social issues, including violence against women and girls. Media, both traditional and digital, shapes how society understands this violence and how institutions respond to it. It can reinforce harmful norms by framing violence as a private matter, or it can challenge them.

Social media has also changed how cases are reported and responded to. A turning point came in 2018, when a journalist was harassed on her way to work and shared her experience online. The post sparked a national conversation in which many women described their own experiences with street harassment. The public outcry led law enforcement to launch joint initiatives on responding to street harassment. “Tell Me Sister,” established in 2020, continues this activism. It documents cases through anonymous submissions, highlights public cases, and calls for accountability for perpetrators and justice for victims.

Traditional media matters too. In my analysis of Asia-Plus, more than half of the 59 relevant articles (32) were feature articles, not just news reports. They covered support services for survivors, government commitments, regional trends, and law enforcement responses, so they were informing the public about solutions as well as incidents.

The 2013 Law on the Prevention of Domestic Violence treats domestic violence as an administrative offense rather than a crime, and other forms of gender-based violence are not defined in either code. Does this legal foundation affect how law enforcement handles domestic violence?

Yes, it does. Criminalization is the first step toward protecting victims and holding perpetrators accountable. Without it, domestic violence is more likely to be treated as a family matter rather than as a crime. Because there is no dedicated offense, cases are prosecuted under general provisions such as hooliganism, bodily harm, or torture, which do not capture the specific nature of domestic violence. The same applies to femicide. The concept does not exist in Tajik law, so these killings are prosecuted under general murder articles that ignore the gender dimension.

My data on police communication shows this. Of the 16 relevant posts on the DushanbePolice Instagram account, only four stated the article under which the perpetrator was prosecuted, and most of those were hooliganism provisions. In one case, police dismissed a domestic violence complaint as “not proven” even though the victim had provided photos of her injuries.

The lack of criminalization also affects data. Tajikistan has no unified system for recording domestic violence and other forms of gender-based violence. Sources also tell very different stories. The U.N. estimates that around 80 percent of women experience domestic violence in their lifetime, while the 2023 Demographic and Health Survey found 12 percent of women aged 15-49 had experienced physical or sexual violence. Official complaints are rising (1,569 in the first half of 2024, against 1,504 in all of 2023), but many victims never report because of fear and stigma, so the real scale remains hidden.
For these reasons, criminalizing domestic violence and other forms of violence against women is essential to ensuring accountability and justice.
Why did you focus on Asia-Plus and the DushanbePolice Instagram account?
My research looks at both media and law enforcement responses, so I chose one leading source from each side.

Asia-Plus is one of the most widely read news agencies in Tajikistan, and its coverage of gender-based violence matters. It was an Asia-Plus journalist who reported the 2018 street harassment case that prompted a national conversation. I analyzed its Russian-language articles from January 2023 to October 2024. A keyword search returned 2,156 results, and after screening, 59 articles were directly relevant.

The Ministry of Internal Affairs is responsible for investigating both administrative and criminal cases, and its DushanbePolice Instagram account is the main public source of information on law enforcement responses. I screened 561 posts from the same period, and 16 dealt with sexual and gender-based violence. The account also draws heavy public commentary, particularly on gender-based violence and female content creators, which makes it useful for understanding public attitudes as well as police practice.

Your conclusions note that media coverage of sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) tended to be reactive, often linked to external triggers. What triggers did you see, and what does this say about how Tajik media covers SGBV?

My research found that coverage of SGBV fluctuated, with spikes witnessed during external events/factors. For instance, during the United Nations’ 16 days of activism against gender-based violence campaign in December 2023, coverage of SGBV rose. Six articles were published in that month alone, with focus on CEDAW (the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women) and toxic masculinity. Coverage also spiked during the high-profile case of the killing of Saltantat Nukeova in Kazakhstan in November 2023.

This trend suggests that SGBV is covered when there is an event, a campaign, or a prominent person involved, not as an ongoing social issue. Coverage is also heavily gendered in authorship. Women wrote 38 of the 59 articles, none were written by men, and the rest of the authors remained unknown. The issue seems to be treated as a “women’s topic” rather than a matter for the whole newsroom and society. The consequence is that public attention rises and falls with the news cycle, which makes sustained pressure for policy change harder.
What should Tajik media and law enforcement do to better cover and address SGBV, and what steps should the government take?

Awareness-raising must continue, but in an ethical, gender-sensitive, trauma-informed, and victim-centered way. Some outlets sensationalize cases, especially extreme violence against children. Journalists should follow the “do no harm” principle and obtain informed consent, particularly when the survivor is still in contact with the perpetrator. Newsrooms should also move from event-driven reporting to sustained coverage, and involve more male journalists, so that gender-based violence is not seen as only a women’s issue.

Law enforcement should recognize domestic violence as a crime and investigate complaints properly, instead of dismissing them as a private and/or family matter. They also need gender-sensitive training, more female officers, more resources, and real accountability mechanisms. Perpetrators must be held accountable. Tajikistan has a dedicated domestic violence law, but the international community recognizes that violence against women should be criminalized, and domestic violence, other forms of gender-based violence, and femicide should be defined in the criminal code. The government should also set up a unified system for collecting and publishing gender-disaggregated data.
Violence against women is not an isolated problem but a continuum. It can begin as gender discrimination, escalate into violence, and in the worst cases end in femicide.
Was there anything that surprised you in your research?

I was both surprised and not surprised by the amount of victim blaming and shaming in public commentary on social media. It shows how much work remains to educate Tajik society about gender-based violence, especially harassment and domestic violence.
